thoughts: French “a” is usually a pure open “ah” vowel (no English-style glide). It can also become a nasal vowel when it’s followed by n/m that isn’t fully pronounced (as in -an/-am), which is a common source of confusion for English speakers.
description:
Most of the time, French **a** is /a/: like the **a** in English *father*, but typically shorter, a bit more front in the mouth, and not turned into a diphthong. Avoid the English *cat* /æ/.

English has no true nasal vowels, so this is usually learned rather than already “known.”
description:
Most of the time, **"on" = /ɔ̃/**: a nasal vowel somewhat like the vowel in English **“law”** said while letting air flow through your nose—**and you do not pronounce an N sound**. Keep lips rounded and avoid ending with an English-style “ng.”

If **"on" is followed by a vowel sound** (e.g., in *Monaco*) or if the N is **doubled** ("onn"), it’s **not nasal**: you pronounce a regular **/ɔ/** (like “off” without the f) **plus an actual N** (/ɔn/).
